Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Mauritania predominantly use paper-based recording for patient data, including handwritten registries and documents patients carry between visits. Health posts submit paper summaries to centers, where aggregate data is entered into DHIS2 for national reporting—no electronic medical records (EMR) or point-of-care digital systems at rural facilities.World Bank PHC Assessment (2019-2022) Digital systems like DHIS2 are used for upward aggregate reporting from district level, but not patient-level recording at clinics.BMC Health Services Research (2021) Recent national Digital Health Strategy (2023+) aims for shared records and facility digitization, but remains aspirational with no evidence of majority rural adoption by 2026; pilots if any are isolated.Digital Watch Observatory Key barriers: poor rural infrastructure (electricity, internet), limited training/staff, vast desert geography, nomadic populations. Gap: National policy emphasizes HMIS aggregation; rural point-of-service lags, relying on manual processes despite ambitions.

The cited sources (World Bank PHC Assessment, BMC Health Services Research, Digital Watch Observatory) remain relevant and consistent with facility-level recording being paper-based while DHIS2 aggregation happens above the facility - per variable guidance, upstream digitisation should not count. revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Mauritania overwhelmingly rely on paper-based recording, including handwritten registries and documents that patients carry between visits. Health posts submit paper summaries to district centres, where data is entered into DHIS2 for national reporting, but this aggregation occurs above facility level and does not reflect point-of-care digitisation. Mauritania's National e-Health Strategy (2024-2030), launched in October 2025, sets out ambitions for a national vaccination database, an E-CNAM digital insurance platform and expanded telemedicine, but these initiatives remain in early implementation and are not yet reflected in routine rural clinic record-keeping. A small NGO-supported pilot has introduced smartphone-based digital data capture for community health workers in nine facilities across two districts, but this remains an isolated exception rather than a national pattern. Poor rural electricity and internet infrastructure, workforce shortages and vast desert geography continue to constrain point-of-service digitisation.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Mauritania, primarily served by the Gendarmerie Nationale, record case files, complaints, and incident reports on paper. UK FCDO prisoner pack describes arrest statements as handwritten "procès-verbal" in local language at basic stations lacking electricity/office equipment and with low literacy UK GOV Prisoner Pack. US State Dept 2022 HR report notes UN HRC finding of poorly maintained police detainee records, indicating manual systems State Dept HR Report. No evidence of digital case management at station level; justice sector digitisation efforts (e.g., Morocco coop 2025, govt reform) are central/court-focused, not rural police. Official gendarmerie site shows no digital tools for records Gendarmerie MR. Francophone context supports paper-based "procès-verbaux" standard.

The three original sources (UK FCDO prisoner pack, US State Dept 2022 human rights report, Gendarmerie website) remain valid and support paper-based record-keeping at station level. Fresh searches on gendarmerie organisation, OSAC security reporting and the 2025 justice-sector digitisation programme found no evidence of digital case management at rural station level; the March 2025 launch of an online criminal-record (casier judiciaire) portal is a central judicial-record system, not facility-level recording at rural police or gendarmerie posts. revised_comments: Rural policing in Mauritania is primarily the responsibility of the Gendarmerie Nationale, which maintains posts across small towns and rural areas alongside a national police force concentrated mainly in urban centres. Case files, complaints and arrest statements (procès-verbaux) at rural stations are recorded by hand, typically at posts that often lack reliable electricity or office equipment. The US State Department's 2022 human rights report notes that detainee records held by police and gendarmerie were poorly maintained, consistent with manual record-keeping. Recent government digitisation efforts, such as the March 2025 launch of an online criminal-record (casier judiciaire) portal accessible via the Houwiyeti app, are centred on national judicial records rather than case management at individual rural police or gendarmerie posts, and do not extend to facility-level digital recording.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Mauritania's civil registration is managed by ANRPTS through Citizens' Reception Centres (CAC) across the country, including rural areas. UNICEF CRVS profile (2017) states birth registration processing is "Electronically," but requires paper extracts from health facilities for registration at local CACs within 60 days. No evidence of direct digital recording at rural points; likely paper declarations entered digitally centrally, consistent with many African CRVS where local sites use paper and aggregate later. Recent digital ID pilots (e-ID, Houwiyeti app for verification) indicate national digitization push but not facility-level recording. Low completeness rates (World Bank data) and rural connectivity challenges (UNDP) support predominantly paper at rural registries with central digital processing. Score 2: predominantly paper locally, some digital aggregation/pilots.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) is not well supported: the row's own Comments field already flagged an internal inconsistency, arguing for a score of 2 despite the recorded Value Code of 1. Independent research into how ANRPTS Citizens' Reception Centres (CAC) actually process registrations - an academic case study (ebrary.net) and a peer-reviewed article in Politique africaine, corroborated by a Canadian IRB research report and ANRPTS's own Houwiyeti launch announcement - shows that, while paper source documents (birth register extract, marriage certificate) are required as inputs, the registering agent enters biographic data directly into a national digital database and captures biometrics (fingerprint, photo) on the spot at the CAC counter. This is facility-level digital data capture, not merely upstream aggregation of paper records, and mobile CAC missions extend the same digital process to villages. This justifies raising the score to 3 (Mostly digital - some paper): paper documents remain necessary as source evidence, but the substantive act of recording happens digitally at the facility. This is a two-step change from the original score of 1, based on three independent, mutually consistent sources describing the same process; it is not a promotion to the top of the scale (4), but given the scale of the change this row is flagged for human review. Year set to 2023, based on the Houwiyeti launch and the most recent operational description of the CAC network; medium-high confidence.
revised_comments: Mauritania's civil status records are managed by the Agence Nationale du Registre de la Population et des Titres Sécurisés (ANRPTS) through a national network of Citizens' Reception Centres (Centres d'Accueil des Citoyens, CAC), which by late 2023 numbered around 150-180 fixed and mobile sites, including mobile missions that travel to villages and residential areas to register rural residents. Registering a birth, for example, requires the parent to bring paper source documents - an extract from the health facility's birth register and the parents' marriage certificate - but CAC staff enter the biographic details directly into the national biometric database at the counter, and biometric data (fingerprints, photograph, signature) is captured digitally on the spot. The process therefore combines a paper-based input step with facility-level digital recording, though frequent power cuts and internet outages in rural areas can interrupt the digitisation process. The ANRPTS-run Houwiyeti mobile application, launched in December 2023, further extends online access to identity and civil status document requests.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Mauritania operates a national EMIS called SIRAGE, supported by World Bank projects, operational across 72 decentralized units and used as the single tool for sector data collection including enrollment and transition rates.World Bank BESSP Phase 2 Annual Statistical Yearbook produced from EMIS data.UNESCO IICBA Country Brief No evidence of digital recording at rural primary school level for attendance, enrollment, grades; rural areas lack infrastructure. Standard EMIS practice involves paper collection at schools, digital aggregation at district level. Recent digital teaching pilots (2024-25) do not indicate facility-level data digitalisation. Score 2: Predominantly paper with digital aggregate reporting.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed, though the row's own Comments text argued (inconsistently with the recorded Value Code) for a score of 2. Per the variable's guidance that digitisation of paper data at a higher level should not count towards the facility-level score, fresh evidence on the 2025 rollout of the SIRAGE education information system (Agence Mauritanienne d'Information coverage of training workshops in Brakna and Hodh Charghi regions, April 2025) shows that school-level data is still gathered via field visits and entered onto the platform by regional inspection staff - i.e. digitisation happens above the facility, not within the rural school itself. No evidence was found of routine digital data capture (e.g. via the companion SIRAGE RIM app) inside individual rural primary schools. The recorded score of 1 is therefore the better-supported reading of the evidence and is confirmed rather than raised to 2. Year set to 2025, based on the most recent SIRAGE rollout reporting; high confidence.
revised_comments: Mauritania's national Education Management Information System, SIRAGE (Système d'Information pour la Réforme Administrative et la Gestion de l'Éducation), is used to compile enrolment, attendance and transition statistics across the decentralised education system. In practice, data on individual rural primary schools is gathered through periodic field missions, in which regional education inspectors and staff visit schools to collect and update information before entering it onto the SIRAGE platform at district or regional level; day-to-day attendance and pupil records at rural primary schools themselves continue to be kept on paper. Training workshops held in the Brakna and Hodh Charghi regions in April 2025 focused on building regional-level capacity to operate SIRAGE and to organise these school-visit data-collection missions, rather than on installing digital recording tools inside individual schools. A companion mobile application, SIRAGE RIM, is marketed to teachers, school administrators, pupils and parents for tracking attendance and academic progress, but there is no evidence of its adoption in rural schools specifically. Rural connectivity constraints further limit prospects for direct facility-level digital recording.
